newsitem.title: GERMANY: East Germany spy-swap lawyer Vogel acquitted.
newsitem.headline: East Germany spy-swap lawyer Vogel acquitted.

text.p: Wolfgang Vogel, a shadowy East Berlin lawyer who arranged superpower spy swaps during the Cold War, was acquitted on Friday by a Berlin court of charges that he blackmailed East Germans trying to emigrate to the West.
The state court ruled prosecutors failed to prove Vogel extorted money from East Germans in exchange for their exit from the former communist state.
"This ruling shows the history of German-German relations, especially in humanitarian matters, still has to be written," Vogel said after the acquittal was read in a packed courtroom.
"I would love to contribute to the writing of that history, but not with the state prosecutor breathing down my back."
Friday's case was linked to another court decision in January when Vogel was convicted of blackmailing people wanting to leave the East and of perjury and falsifying documents.
The 71-year-old Vogel has appealed that ruling, which cost him two years probation and a 92,000 mark ($63,500) fine.

Vogel was a close confidant of former East German leader Erich Honecker and one of the former Soviet bloc's rare millionaires. He was a regular fixture at Cold War spy exchanges -- often arriving in his golden Mercedes.

During his 30-year career as an unofficial East-West go-between he secured the release of more than 100 agents. The 71-year-old Vogel started the exchanges with the 1962 spy swap between U.S. pilot Gary Powers and Soviet spy Rudolf Abel.
But he also helped shepherd nearly 34,000 political prisoners and 215,000 East Germans to freedom in the west, a lucrative trade that earned him the nickname "devil's advocate."

Vogel, a suave attorney with a passion for clocks and cars, delivered an estimated 3.5 billion marks ($2.3 billion) in hard currency from Bonn to the impoverished East in exchange for the release of political prisoners.
He also earned hefty fees in both West German and East German marks, which triggered accusations he was a greedy opportunist -- charges he rejected.
"I have just learned that in a state under the rule of law, people are not left exposed to the whims of a state prosecutor," said Vogel.
The second trial was started after prosecutors decided the first trial was growing cumbersome.
But much of the evidence was weak and acquittal became likely after several prosecution witnesses testified Vogel did not profit from their desire to leave for the West.
Prosecutors were seeking a 4-1/2 year prison term. They had charged Vogel of forcing East German emigrants to sell their houses and property at bargain prices to the Communist elite.
Vogel steadfastly denied the charges, saying he was merely a mediator trying to help people.

"Those wanting to emigrate went voluntarily to Vogel and brought their money or property into play," Judge Heinz Holzinger said. "Vogel cannot be held responsible for the imhumane emigration policies of East Germany. He was not a state decision-maker."
But Vogel is not entirely in the clear yet. He still faces one more trial -- for tax evasion.
